notes: Puzzle leads because the prompt self-declares an escape room and the run is gated by a keycard and a door; Survival is named second and supplied the monster and the exit rows.

Shape: Puzzle's rooms-sequence assumes rooms worked through in a fixed order, and this house is explored freely with the keycard in a random bedroom. interior-single fits better — the house is the whole map and the player never goes outside, so there is no exterior to generate and no P3.

Survival's warren-looping was the close call. It routes P6 and guarantees zero dead ends, which is what a pathfinding chase normally needs — but this house has bedrooms, and a bedroom is a dead end by definition. Built as a plain interior; say the word and the hallways can be looped instead, which is a procedural-first build.
The monster is slower than walking, so corridor width matters less than usual — no minimum passing width has been imposed beyond ordinary hallway sizing.

notes_for_us: The prompt is an escape room with a chasing monster, and the two genres disagree about the shape: Puzzle wants sealed chambers in order, Survival wants a dead-end-free warren at P6. The skill's boundary note treats them as mutually exclusive — 'the pressure is a pursuing threat, not a locked door' — but here it is provably both, and the boundary rule gives no way to hold them together.

There is no plain player-spawn option. spawn-protected is for asymmetric roles, spawn-grid for racing, spawn-teambase for shooters, spawn-first-reveal for showcases. A single spawn point, which this prompt names outright, had to be free text with a hand-chosen SpawnZone type.
The plank is a three-click destructible barrier and had to be split across gate-progression for the block and a free-text TriggerZone for the clicking. Neither row is really it.

mechanics: Grid-based incremental: place mushrooms on an 8x8 grid to generate spores per second

Pop Shrooms generate 1 spore per second but fire the pop effect 10 times instead of once when popped
